FROM OUR STATE EXCHANGES.
A knitting factory, with a capital of $25,000, is to be established at Madison.

A petition is in circulation for the removal of the land office from Menasha to Oconto.

The aggregate loss by the Durand fire is stated to be $50,000 and the insurance $10,000.

Arrangements are being made for starting a paper mill with a capital of $25,000 at Eau Claire.

Over 1,000 names were secured to the pledge during the recent temperance revival in Whitewater.

A young man, named Leonard, was killed by a falling tree in Emmet Horan's lumber camp on the Eau Claire, on the 20th.

The loss by the burning of Kickbusch's sash and blind factory, at Wausau, recently, was $15,000. The insurance was but $2,000.

Simon Ottoson was robbed of a gold watch and a sum of money by two highwaymen in Racine a night or two ago. No clue to the robbers.

Considerable attention is being given to the improvement of sheep in some portions of Sheboygan county, especially in the vicinity of Hingham.

Green Bay Gazette: A gentleman from Marquette informs the reporter of the Gazette that the weather in that region reminded one of spring; clear water was seen over the lake and several tugs were plying between different points.

Mr. Wm. Grenzow, of Spring Grove, had $46 stolen out of a bureau drawer in
MR. WM. GRENZOW, of Spring Grove, had $46 stolen out of a bureau drawer in his house while he was attending church in this village last Sunday. The preacher was right in saying that members should bring their pocket books to church.

SPARTA HEBALD: Mr. Simeon S. Snattuck, living northwest of town, was presented with a broken leg for Christmas. Sunday morning he attempted jumping across a small stream, alighting on his right foot, and falling backward on the left, breaking the leg below the knee.

FOND DU LAC Commonwealth: A rumor reaches this city that Charles LaFour, who is well-known in police circles here, killed a man at Superior City, Lake Superior, and was lynched by a mob. An effort was made to-day to get the truth in the matter, but nothing certain has yet been learned.

STEVENS POINT Gazette: The Green Bay, Stevens Point and Northern R. R. has entered the city and rails have been laid as far as Owen Clark's lumber office. We are now connected with an iron band on this route with Green Bay on the east and Winona, Minn., on the west, giving us railroad facilities second to no city in this section of the state, and still the day is not far distant until we will have another road and perhaps two.

EAU CLAIRE News: John Powell, aged 83, a resident of the town of Brunswick, was drowned on Saturday last in a small lake near his residence. It seems the old gentleman went out on the ice to fish and venturing out too near the open water the ice gave way and he fell in. No one being present, he was unable to get out and soon drowned. As he did not return at the usual time his son went out in search of him and was soon horror-struck at finding the place where he broke through. Procuring assistance, the body was rescued. The funeral took place on Monday.

GREEN BAY Daily Data: A sad case of desertion is that related by Mrs. Rika Klein, who has been in this part of the state for the past two weeks in search of her husband Henry Klein, alias Henry Wolf, who has abandoned her to abscond with a woman to whom he had been engaged before marrying his present wife. The injured wife traced the pair to Menasha, but there lost track of them. She learned, however, that they had been married, without Henry's having gone through the formality of procuring a divorce. Mrs. Klein is very anxious to discover the whereabouts of Klein, as she and her children are left in strait-ened circumstances. The injured wife has given up the search, and left last evening over the Northwestern road for her home in Milwaukee.

EAU CLAIRE Free Fress, December 24th: We were informed on Friday evening, by Mr. William Ebner, just arrived in this city, that on the morning of the 20th inst. a barn and shed owned by the Knapp, Stout & Co. company, at Twenty-two-mile Ford, 22 miles north of Menomonie, were burned to the ground, entailing a loss estimated at $4,000; that the entire contents, comprising six horses, six mules, harnesses, two carriages, reapers, mowers and other farm machinery, and 1,500 bushels of oats, burned with the buildings; that a belief prevailed that the fire was the work of an incendiary, as the fumes of kerosene were noticed around the burning premises while the fire was raging; that the clearing out of the ruins is going on now, and that the company will rebuild the destroyed structures immediately.

Big Springs.
Special to the Herald.
Big Springs, March 27.—About ten days since six negro convicts escaped from a gang working for the Texas & Pacific out west, killing one guard. They robbed a camp on the Texas & Pacific, and secured arms, rations, and civilians' clothing. Two made their way safely to Mexico, and the other four traveled east along the road, pursued by Captain McMurray's rangers. They broke into several section-houses for rations. Saturday the sergeant came upon them lying in the brush near the roadway and ordered them to hold up their hands. They ran off, and two were killed and the other two captured.

Convicts Escaped-Three Killed.
Convicts Escaped—Three Killed.
GALVESTON, March 27.—Six colored convicts, working on the Texas Pacific road, killed the guard and escaped. Two got into Mexico. The others were pursued and two killed and two captured.

Latest by Mail.
Chicago, March 28.—Six cases of small-pox and four deaths.

Cincinnati, March 28.—Forty cases of small-pox were reported to-day and five deaths, the largest number yet reported.

Vicksburg, March 28.—The Yazoo and Tallahatchie rivers are falling. The further distribution of supplies continues. Two negroes were drowned at Forest house to-day.

San Francisco, March 28.—Reports from the interior indicate that the grain crops will be rather better than the average in nearly all counties except those in the San Joaquin valley.

Davenport, March 28.—The state central committee of the anti-prohibition association met here to-day for a conference with a full attendance, and adjourned to meet at Des Moines Wednesday, April 27.

Big Springs, Tex., March 28.—Six negro convicts escaped from a working gang on the Texas Pacific road, killing one of the guards. Officers came upon them in camp and two were killed and the rest captured.

New Orleans, March 28.—A correspondent of the Times-Democrat from Musson, La., says 200 square miles of land, occupied by 4,000 people is under water.

Denver, March 28—'The News' Leadville special says J. C. Early, an attorney and well known politician, this evening shot and killed Policeman Samuel Townsend. The quarrel was over the costs in a replevin suit. An attempt to lynch Early was frustrated.

Chicago, March 28.—The Canadian visitors have concluded their programme of sight-seeing, and now expect to divide into three parties, one division going to Winnipeg, via St. Paul, the other to St. Louis and the third to Omaha, Kansas City and perhaps Denver.

TELEGRAPHIC NEWS
Criminal Calendar.
Louisville, 29.—An unknown maniac shot and killed Alex. C. Swingate, of Langton, on the Ohio and Missouri train near Mendota, Indiana, this morning. The assassin then jumped from the train while going forty miles an hour, landed safely, walked half a mile to a creek, stripped and jumped in, drowning himself. Some money and whisky were found on his person.

Deadwood, D. T., 29—Crow Dog, recently convicted of the murder of Spotted Tail, was to-day sentenced to be hanged on May 11th.

Chicago; 28.—Edward Streher, a saloon keeper of unsavory reputation, shot and killed a young expressman named Wm. Mitchell, in his saloon, 144 West Lake street to-night.

St. Petersburg, 28.—The chief of the Nihilist's executive committee, connected with the construction of the mine in Little Garden street, is arrested.

Charleston, 28.—The election cases which begun on Monday number twenty; number of defendants, 56. All the defendants in Richland, Sumter, Georgetown, and Colleton, and three in Charleston, were commissioners or managers of the election.

St. Louis, 29.—R. J. Bowman, late county Judge of Phelps County, fired a load of buckshot into the body of Alfred Hayes, last night, as he was walking a street in the little town of St. James. It was a regular assassination, Hayes being aken entirely unaware.

W. M. Stack, a bully who murdered a man on the race track at Chicago a few years ago, shot Martin Monahan, in a political row in Kansas, last night.

G Bockerout, a reputable citizen of Artico, Texas, was called out of his house a night or two ago by W. W. Parks, his son Theodore, and a man named Bowles, and riddled with bullets. The affair grew out of a law suit in which Parks got worsted.

Chicago, 29.—Evening Journal's Pine Bluffs, Arkansas special: Mrs. Ballard, of Lincoln County, after a disagreement with her husband on Monday morning, took her children, aged 7 and 4 years, and a four months old infant, and repaired to a pond near her home, where she broke the neck of the two oldest, threw the bodies in the pond, and drowned herself and the infant. The family were respectable.

Dublin, 29.—Four additional arrests in connection with the shooting of McMahon. Ammunition and rifles were seized. Supposed Fenian documents were also captured in the house of one of the assailants whose father and two brothers have been arrested.

Chicago, 24.—Pokewell, arrested in Wisconsin for horse stealing, and bank forgery, was sentenced at Sidney, Iowa, yesterday, to ten years in the penitentiary on the forgery charge.

Big Springs, Texas, 28.—Six negro convicts escaped from a gang working on the Texas and Pacific Railroad, killing one guard. They robbed the camp and secured arms, rations and civilian clothing. Two made their way to Mexico and the other four traveled east along the road, pursued by rangers. The rangers came upon them lying in the brush. They ran and two were killed and the others captured.

Dallas, 28.—Detective Jack Duncan left, to-day, for Arizona to secure Frank Jackson, the most desperate member of the Samuel Bass gang of train robbers. Jackson has been at large since his fight at Round Rock, in '78, in which Samuel Bass, S. E. Barnes and others were killed. Positive information has been received that Jackson has been lurking between Los Vegas, Tucson. Tombstone and Prescott since November, at the head of a gang of desperadoes. There is a standing reward of $2,500 for Jackson.

RIDDLED WITH BULLETS.
ATROCIOUS MURDER IN TEN-
NESSEE.
A Revenue Officer Shot Down by a
Band of Moonshiners From Ambush-Thirty Wounds in His Body.
NASHVILLE, March 12.—A special from McMinnville says: "J. M. Davis, the celebrated raider of moonshiners, was wayiaid and killed this afternoon about three miles from McMinnville. Thos. Vickers, who was with Davis, says there were twenty men in the gang that did the shooting."

Davis was a Deputy United States Revenue Collector. His body was brought to McMinnville this evening after an inquest had been held. His assassins were concealed behind a pile of logs, covered with freshly cut cedar boughs, and were armed with shotguns and pistols. Vickers, the companion of Davis, was riding by his side, and a man named Campbell and others of the revenue party were following about a quarter of a mile behind. When Davis was shot off his horse Vickers galloped back to the others, and Campbell and his party coming up, the brush and put his pistol to Davis' head and shoot. Oyster cans were found behind the ambuscade freshly opened. They had been purchased in McMinnville, at Martin's store. Davis' brains were shot out, and there were over thirty bullet holes in his body.
james-m-davis-mcminnville-1882-03-13.A3: Deputy U. S. revenue collector Davis was shot dead near McMinnville, Saturday evening by moonshiners.

james-m-davis-mcminnville-1882-03-13.A11:
The Murdered Deputy Collector.
DETAILS OF THE KILLING OF JAMES M. DAVIS BY
MOONSHINERS IN TENNESSEE.
Deputy Collector James M. Davis of the inter
The Murdered Deputy Collector.
DETAILS OF THE KILLING OF JAMES M. DAVIS BY MOONSHINERS IN TENNESSEE.

Deputy Collector James M. Davis, of the internal revenue service, who was waylaid and murdered by moonshiners near Nashville, Tenn., a few days ago, was one of the most valuable men in the service. The commissioner of internal revenue says he never hesitated to do his duty, no matter what the odds, and that he was as brave as a lion. He has long been a terror to moonshiners, and they have been trying hard to get him out of the way. About a year ago he had his hip broken and his skull fractured in two places. Commissioner Raum ordered him here at once, and he was under the care of Dr. Bliss for some time. He entirely recovered from his injuries, and since has done good work. His assassination is quite a blow to the internal revenue service. Although Commissioner Raum is anxious to bring the assassins to justice, it is generally believed in Tennessee that the reward of $300 for each is insufficient to secure their arrest, as all are regarded as desperate men, well used to handling firearms.

A gentleman, who arrived at Nashville from the mountains a few days ago, said that if Davis had had half a chance he would singly and alone have fought his assassins, eight to twelve in number; was riding without a saddle girth, which had been lost, so that when the horse jumped at the first fire he was thrown to the ground. He lay on the earth as if dead for a short time, having been hit in the leg. He finally got up and started back limping, when the bushwhackers began to fire at him and he again fell prostrate. One of the assassins then walked up upon the embankment and shot the top of his head off with a double-barrelled shotgun. Davis and his prisoner. Vickers, were allowed to pass the ambuscade before the murderers fired upon him. It was thought that this was done in order to get Vickers out of range of their shots. Davis, wounded as he was, fired three shots, while U. S. Commissioner Campbell, who was 150 yards behind, fired one shot. After they had killed Davis the party departed, taking a path leading over Ben Lomond Mountain, above McMinnville, whence they came. They were seen in the suburbs of McMinnville on the morning preceding the assassination and some persons talking to them. One hundred shots were fired. Twenty-six bullet holes were found in the back portion of Davis' coat.
james-m-davis-mcminnville-1882-03-13.A14:
Capt. Jas. M. Davis Killed.
Deputy Collector Davis and his men were returning from Beersheba Springs to this place Monday last, and when about three miles from here Davis was fired upon by some parties in ambush. At the first fire Thomas Vickers, who was riding with Davis, fled. When shot Davis fell from his horse, but soon regained his feet and started back up the road toward Campbell and Cathcart who were in the rear. He had not gone far, however, when he was fired upon again and killed. An inquest was held and the body was brought to town. Between twenty and thirty bullets were found in the body and the skull was litterally shattered with pistol balls.

The shooting was done by men concealed behind breastworks constructed of logs and cord-wood and covered over with cedar brush. This structure was about ten feet from the Beersheba road and the underbrush had been cut away so as to leave an unobstructed view. The assaulting party is estimated at from 10 to 15 men, George Campbell, who has been with Davis a long time, and was with him on this trip, states that Davis' conduct was very strange for two or three days prior to his death, that he manifested signs of restlessness and depression altogether unusual in him. Vickers states that Davis was laughing and telling a long anecdote when he rode into the deadly ambush and the shooting began.

The following we take from the Nashville Banner of Tuesday:

James M. Davis was a native of Tennessee, and was about 35 years of age. He was 6 feet 2½ inches tall, large boned and muscular and weighed 210 pounds. Although possessing great physical strength and courage, he was kind-hearted and gentle. During his career in the revenue service he arrested nearly 3,500 violators of the law.

Prior to his employment by the United States, about 11 years ago, Davis was engaged by the state of Tennessee in recapturing escaped penitentiary convicts and ar-
Prior to his employment by the United States, about 11 years ago, Davis was engaged by the state of Tennessee in recapturing escaped penitentiary convicts and arresting horse thieves with which the State was cursed directly after the war. While in the service of the government he cut up and destroyed about 1,000 moonshine distilleries.

During his career as an officer of the government he was forced to kill several men in self defense.

Davis, when a mere youth, entered the Confederate army and made a good soldier. It is understood that Davis was warned two weeks ago that men were lying in wait for him for the purpose of killing him. He leaves a wife and several children.

His life was insured, it is said for $14,000.

The following telegram was received by Collector Woodcock.

WASHINGTON, D. C., March 14.

W. M. Woodcock, Nashville:

Offer a reward of $300 each for the arrest of the men engaged in the assassination of Deputy Collector J. M. Davis. You are authorized to expend $500 for the discovery of these conspirators. Leave nothing undone for their arrest under section 5,918 U. S. Revised Statutes. If necessary reinforce marshall's posse with your deputies for the arrest of these men. The funeral expenses of Deputy Collector Davis will be paid.

GREEN B. RAUM,
Collector.
james-m-davis-mcminnville-1882-03-13.A15:
DAVIS' DEATH.
A Presentiment Which Made Him Restive.
It appears that Davis had a presentiment that he would be killed before he got off the mountains. In consequence he was restive from the time he left McMinnville. When he had reached a point not far from the ambuseade on the Beersheba road, Vickers says Davis called his attention to some loose horses on Ben Lomond mountain, but Vickers could not observe them. Davis had been to Beersheba and was on his way to McMinnville. His assassins had come over the point at Ben Lomond mountain. At one place on the mountain the road to the rear could be observed for a distance of two miles. When Davis and his men came in sight, on this part of the road, a pistol shot was fired. This was believed to have been a signal to the assassins that Davis and his men had come in sight, and for them to make all the necessary arrangements to kill him. The shooting did not occur until half an hour after the signal. Before reaching the ambuseade Davis got Vickers to get down and let out his stirrup straps, that he might simply touch the stirrups with his toes. The ambush was so constructed that each one of the eight men had a porthole through which he could fire, the base of it being a large log, with wings, made of cord wood, thrown out in front and on each side, and covered with cedar. It is believed the oysters, in the cans found, must have been eaten on some day previous to the assassination. It is said that in their testimony before the coroner's jury, two wood-choppers within fifteen feet of whom the assassins passed, denied having known the men. The white man testified that he thought he knew five of the men when they were approaching him, but he was satisfied he did not know any of them after they had passed by him. The negro testified that he did not know any of the men in the crowd and could not identify any one of them. They came upon him and his white companion so unexpectedly that he was scared and said to them out of fear, perhaps, more than anything else, "we surrender," supposing they had come after them, but why he could not tell. None of the men said anything, and went off in another direction.

It is thought that the two wood choppers, even if they had recognized any of the men, would not dare to say so from fear of the vengeance of the assassins or their friends. It will thus be very difficult to discover the men who killed Davis.

Some men are suspected of having taken part in the assassination, but it is doubtless whether the real assassins will ever be found.—[American.

ouidas-bailey-cuthbert-1882-02-28.A1:
A GEORGIA TRAGEDY.
A Young White Buffalo Shot by a Negro whose House he had Invaded.

CUTHBERT, Ga., March 3.—On Tuesday night four masked men went to the house of a negro living in this county and demanded admittance. Upon being refused they broke down the door, and as the first man entered the negro shot him. The men then fled. The negro, with some white neighbors, tracked the wounded man for some distance and finally found his dead body. Upon removing the mask he was found to be a young white man, belonging to the county, named Leonidas Bailey. The other three men are unknown. The object of their visit has not been ascertained.

WASHINGTON, March 3.—O'Neil, of Pennsylvania, presented a resolution of the tobacco board of trade of Philadelphia, asking that congress either pass promptly a bill for the abolition of the tax on tobacco and cigars, or agree to a joint resolution to the effect that it is unwise to tamper with the tax during the present congress; also a resolution of the Philadelphia board of marine underwriters, in favor of a bill putting the signal service of the United States army on a permanent basis. Both resolutions were referred.

Gibson, of Louisiana, introduced a bill making appropriations for the construction, repair, completion and preservation of certain work on the Mississippi river in accordance with the recommendation, plans, etc., of the Mississippi river commission. Referred.

It makes an appropriation of $3,113,000 dollars for the initial work for constructing a channel and protecting the caving banks in the reaches of the river, constituting a length of one hundred and eighty-one miles, namely: New Madrid, thirty miles; Memphis reach, sixteen miles; Helena reach, thirty miles; Chatow bend, thirty-five miles, and Lake Providence reach, thirty miles.

It also appropriates $25,000,000 for building and repairing levees and closing the gaps of levees, and $50,000 for fortifications at Atghafa bayou and the mouth of Red river. The resolution was referred.

High as Haman.

New Orleans, March 3.—A special to the Times-Democrat from Aberdeen, Miss., says Robert Jones, white, and Wm. Miller, colored, were hanged there to-day, for the murder of the Walker Bros. in November last. Neither made any remarks. Jones fainted, and was helped up to the rope. The trap fell at 12.04 p. m. Both went down together, and both necks were broken. Life was pronounced extinct in eleven minutes.

Miller said prior to the fall that he expected to go straight to heaven and commenced to sing in a sad, wailing voice.

Shot for a Robber.

DANVILLE, Va., March 3.—Wm. Walker, of Pittsburgh county, was killed at Chatham, at 4 o'clock yesterday morning, by Silas G. Johnson, a merchant's clerk. Walker, who slept with Johnson, went out while the latter was asleep, and in returning awoke Johnson, who, mistal'ng him for a robber, shot him dead with a pistol. The coroner's jury gave a verdict in accordance with this statement.

Tennessee Republicans.

NASHVILLE, March 3.—The state republican committee and prominent republicans met in caucus last night, continuing in session till 1 this morning. They resolved to call the gubernatorial convention to meet April 27th, and favored the call of the constitutional convention for August next. The republicans will adhere to the Hawkins platform, which was to settle the state debt on the best compromise to which the bondholders will submit.

A MASKED MAN SHOT.
On Tuesday night of last week four masked men went to the house of Berry Lawrence, colored, near Cuthbert, Ga., and demanded admission. Upon being refused admission they broke down the door, and as one of the party entered, the negro discharged his gun at him, and the others fled. The negro went to the nearest white neighbor, Mr. D. C. Andrews, and stated the facts. Mr. Andrews came down and looking about found a hat torn with shot and clotted with blood. Getting a torch, he observed traces of blood leading in the direction of the church. In the rear of the church he found the body of a dead man. Other neighbors came in when it was light and the mask was removed from the dead man revealing the faces of Leonidas Bailey. Indications on the ground in front of the negroe's house gave evidence that there had been four horses and a buggy about there the night before. The coroner's jury empanelled gave a verdict of justifiable homicide. Baily was about 30 years old, sober, industrious and respected in the community.

HINDSBORO, Ill., March 29.—A destructive conflagration originated in E. W. Helm's dry goods store, spreading to Abe Miller's store, then to Stork & Hearns' drug store and hardware store, then to Taylor & Simpson's dry good store, completely destroying the houses invaded. TORONTO, March 29.—John Olmer & Co.'s planing mill at Saho, the foundry and a car manufactory company's premises were destroyed by fire this morning. Loss, $60,000.

Killed While Drunk.

National Associated Press.

KANSAS CITY. March 29.—Eugene Chilton was murdered on Tuesday night last by Thomas Eddington near Independence, this county. Chilton was spending the evening with Eddington's daughter. He had a flask of whisky with him and became intoxicated. In that condition he quarrelled with Eddington and attempted to shoot the latter, but was prevented by the daughter The father procured a pistol, put Chilton out of the house and fired at him. Chilton was heard to exclaim: "I am shot," but ran away. The next morning his body was found lying in the road where he had died.

Result of an Old Feud

National Associated Press.

WATERLY, Ohio, MICHIGAN.

Jasper last evening Gilbert Shopshire shot and instantly killed John Ryder and his son George and put a bullet through the arm of Dave, another of Ryder's sons. The tragedy is the sequel of a feud between the families for years. The trouble grew out of the alleged criminal intimacy between Shopshire's wife and Jim Ryder, son of John and brother of George. Great bitterness has grown out of the trial of the case in court.

Mexican Matters.

National Associated Press.

CITY OF MEXICO, March 29.—The authorities have determined to raise by the issuing of bonds $18,000,000, to effect city improvements by the introduction of a system of water pipes, relaying pavements of streets and building of slaughter houses, to be conducted under the management of the city authorities.

Ex-Governor Moses.

National Associated Press.

NEW YORK, March 29.—Franklin J. Moses, ex-governor of South Carolina, was arrested to-day on the charge of swindling Freeber W. Smith, a piano manufacturer, to whom he represented himself as a brother of Gov. Colquit, of Georgia, out of $75. There are quite a number of similar charges against him, and during the day he was identified by several of his victims. To-morrow they will appear against him in the Tombs court.

Murderer Caught
National Associated Press

KANSAS CITY, March 29.—William Stock, who shot Mike Monohan in a saloon in West Kansas City last night, was captured this evening in Kansas About one thousand of Monohan's friends assembled and attempted to lynch the prisoner, but the officers succeeded in grabbing him and lodged him in jail, where he is now safely confined.
